defs: A prefix meaning without, absence of, or not.
A prefix meaning slow, often used in cardiac terms.
A prefix meaning bad, painful, or difficult in medical terms.
A prefix meaning above, excessive, or beyond normal.
A prefix meaning below, beneath, or deficient in medical terms.
A prefix meaning between two or more structures.
A prefix meaning within or inside a structure.
A prefix meaning around or surrounding a structure.
A prefix meaning many or excessive in amount.
A prefix meaning under or beneath a structure.
A prefix meaning rapid or fast, often cardiac.
A prefix meaning one or single in number.

The word root referring to the heart in medical terms.
The word root referring to a body cell.

The word root referring to blood in medical terms.
The word root referring to the color white.

A combining form referring to the heart in medical terms.

subjects.name: Body Systems
defs: The layer of skin between the epidermis and hypodermis, containing connective tissue, blood vessels, and glands.
A widespread sweat gland that produces watery sweat for body temperature regulation.
The outermost tissue layer of the skin, made of epithelial cells.
The connective tissue layer that anchors the skin to underlying bone and muscle.
The most common epidermal cell, which produces keratin for skin strength.
A cell in the deepest epidermal layer that produces the pigment melanin.
A dangerous skin cancer that originates from pigment-producing melanocytes.
A deep skin receptor that detects vibration and deep pressure.
An oil gland in the dermis that secretes sebum to lubricate skin and hair.
The outermost layer of the epidermis, made of dead, flattened cells.
Dense, hard bone tissue that withstands compressive forces.
A cartilage growth plate in immature bone that lengthens the bone.
Blood cell production that occurs in the red marrow of bones.
The synapse where a motor neuron signals a muscle fiber to contract.
A bone cell that synthesizes and secretes new bone matrix.
A bone cell that breaks down and resorbs bone tissue.
The main cell of mature bone, which maintains the mineralized matrix.
A disease in which bone resorption outpaces formation, reducing bone mass.
The repeating contractile unit of skeletal muscle containing actin and myosin.
Light, lattice-like bone tissue that supports shifts in weight.
The largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the heart.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
The smallest blood vessel, where gases and nutrients exchange.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart relaxes and fills.
The percentage of blood volume occupied by red blood cells.
The oxygen-carrying protein found in red blood cells.
The muscular middle layer of the heart wall that pumps blood.
The heart's natural pacemaker that initiates each heartbeat.
The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart contracts.
A blood vessel that returns blood toward the heart.
A tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange occurs.
A major airway branch that carries air into each lung.
The dome-shaped muscle that drives breathing by changing thoracic volume.
The act of pushing air out of the lungs during breathing.
The act of drawing air into the lungs during breathing.
The thin membrane that lines the lungs and chest cavity.
A test measuring how much air the lungs can move.
A substance that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
The windpipe that conducts air between the larynx and bronchi.
The process of moving air into and out of the lungs.
A rapid electrical signal that travels along a neuron's membrane.
The long fiber that carries signals away from a neuron's cell body.
The brain region that coordinates movement and balance.
The largest part of the brain, responsible for higher functions.
A branching fiber that receives signals toward a neuron's cell body.
The fatty sheath that insulates axons and speeds signal conduction.
A nerve cell that transmits electrical signals in the body.
A chemical messenger released across a synapse between neurons.
The nerve bundle that relays signals between brain and body.
The junction where one neuron communicates with another cell.
The muscular sac that stores urine before excretion.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland.
A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose levels.
The organ that filters blood and produces urine.
The organ that produces bile and processes nutrients.
The functional unit of the kidney that filters blood.
The gland that secretes digestive enzymes and insulin.
The organ where most of the body's nutrient absorption occurs.
The muscular organ that mixes food with gastric juice.
An endocrine gland that regulates metabolism and growth.

subjects.name: Clinical Abbreviations
defs: ABG denotes arterial blood gases, a test used to detect lung diseases.
BMI denotes body mass index, a measure of appropriate weight for height.
BP denotes blood pressure, the force of blood against artery walls.
BUN denotes blood urea nitrogen, a blood test for kidney disease.
GFR denotes glomerular filtration rate, a test of kidney damage.
HCT denotes hematocrit, a blood test measurement of red cell volume.
HGB denotes hemoglobin, a blood test measurement of oxygen-carrying protein.
RBC denotes red blood cell, a type of blood cell.
WBC denotes white blood cell, a type of blood cell.
AFIB denotes atrial fibrillation, a disturbance of heart rhythm.
AIDS denotes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, infection caused by HIV.
ALS denotes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease.
CHF denotes congestive heart failure, when the heart cannot pump enough blood.
COPD denotes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a lung disease causing breathlessness.
DVT denotes deep-vein thrombosis, a blood clot in a deep vein.
GERD denotes gastroesophageal reflux disease, when stomach contents leak into the gullet.
HTN denotes hypertension, meaning chronically high blood pressure.
MI denotes myocardial infarction, commonly called a heart attack.
CABG denotes coronary artery bypass graft, a type of heart surgery.
CXR denotes chest x-ray, an imaging test of the lungs.
D&C denotes dilatation and curettage, a surgical procedure on the uterus.
ECG denotes electrocardiogram, a test measuring the heart's electrical impulses.
EEG denotes electroencephalogram, a test measuring the brain's electrical impulses.
MRI denotes magnetic resonance imaging, a type of imaging test.
PAP denotes Papanicolau, a test used to detect cervical cancer.
PET denotes positron emission tomography, a type of imaging test.
DTP denotes diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccine for three diseases.
HRT denotes hormone replacement therapy, replacing hormones the body lacks.
IM denotes intramuscular, a type of injection into muscle.
IV denotes intravenous, a type of injection into a vein.
MMR denotes measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine for three diseases.
NG denotes nasogastric, a tube used to empty stomach contents.
NKDA denotes no known drug allergies in the patient record.
NSAID denotes non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen.
Rx denotes prescription, the written order for medication.
CDC denotes Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, a public health agency.
CNS denotes central nervous system, the brain and spinal cord.
ENT denotes ear, nose, and throat, a clinical specialty.
GI denotes gastrointestinal, another term for the digestive system.
GU denotes genitourinary, the urinary and sex organs.
HCO denotes healthcare organization, a facility delivering care.
HCP denotes healthcare personnel, staff providing patient care.
ICU denotes intensive care unit, a special hospital unit.
BID denotes twice a day, a prescription frequency.
PRN denotes as needed, taken only when symptoms require.
QD denotes daily, an abbreviation on the do-not-use list.
QHS denotes nightly at bedtime, an error-prone abbreviation.
QID denotes four times a day, a prescription frequency.
QOD denotes every other day, an abbreviation on the do-not-use list.
TID denotes three times a day, a prescription frequency.

subjects.name: Documentation
defs: The collection of documents forming a patient's medical record.
Protected health information used to make decisions about a patient's care.
A digital patient record shared across healthcare settings and providers.
A digital record of care created and used within one practice or facility.
Data about a person's health status, care, or payment for care.
The official business record of a healthcare organization released on request.
A documented account of a patient's health history, care, and treatments over time.
The process of recording patient care facts in the medical record.
A health record maintained and controlled by the patient.
The length of time medical records must be kept.
A late entry added to clarify or supplement an existing note.
The clinician's diagnosis or clinical impression of the patient's condition.
A summary of hospital care, findings, and instructions at discharge.
A comprehensive initial assessment of a patient's health and exam.
Measurable clinical findings and test results documented in a note.
The intended tests, treatments, and follow-up for the patient.
A maintained list of a patient's active and resolved health problems.
A dated entry documenting a patient's status and care since the last visit.
A progress note organized into subjective, objective, assessment, and plan sections.
The patient's reported symptoms, concerns, and history in a note.
A group of related orders used for a common clinical situation.
An order to give a medication or treatment as needed.
A clinician's instruction to provide a treatment, test, or medication.
A written or electronic order for a medication to be dispensed.
A repeat dispensing of a prescription without a new order.
The directions on a prescription telling how to take a medication.
A pre-approved order carried out when specified conditions are met.
An order requiring immediate administration or performance of a service.
An order given over the phone and documented for later authentication.
An order spoken aloud and later transcribed into the medical record.
A legal document stating a patient's future healthcare wishes.
A change or addition made to a health record at a patient's request.
The duty to keep patient information private and secure.
A document recording a patient's agreement to a proposed treatment.
A transparent fix to an error in an existing medical record entry.
An order not to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation if the heart stops.
A US law protecting the privacy and security of health information.
Permission given after a patient understands the risks and benefits of care.
A patient's right to control access to their health information.
The process of disclosing health records to authorized requesters.
A code set describing medical procedures and physician services.
A request submitted to a payer for payment of healthcare services.
A code identifying a patient's disease or condition for billing.
A code reporting evaluation and management services by level.
A code set for supplies, equipment, and services not in CPT.
A US diagnosis coding system for classifying diseases and conditions.
The requirement that a service be reasonable and needed for diagnosis or treatment.
A code added to a procedure to show special circumstances.
A code identifying a medical service or procedure performed.
A form listing services and codes used to create a claim.

subjects.name: Diagnostics
defs: Blood tests measuring glucose, electrolytes, and kidney function.
Nitrogen in blood from urea, reflecting kidney function.
Blood level of calcium, a mineral for bones and muscles.
Blood level of chloride, an electrolyte balancing fluids.
A blood test measuring red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Blood test adding liver enzymes and proteins to a basic panel.
Waste product filtered by kidneys, used to assess kidney function.
Amount of sugar present in the blood at testing.
Average blood glucose over the past two to three months.
Percentage of blood volume made up of red blood cells.
Protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
A blood test measuring cholesterol and triglyceride levels.
The number of platelets in a blood sample.
Blood level of potassium, an electrolyte for nerves and muscles.
Number of red blood cells per volume of blood.
Expected interval of test results in healthy people.
Blood level of sodium, an electrolyte regulating fluids.
Number of white blood cells in a blood sample.
The imaging of blood vessels using contrast dye.
Detailed cross-sectional images created from X-rays and computers.
A substance improving visibility of structures in imaging.
A low-dose X-ray measuring the bone mineral density.
Continuous real-time moving X-ray images of the body.
Detailed images using magnetic fields and radio waves.
X-ray imaging of the breast for screening and diagnosis.
Images from small amounts of radioactive tracer material.
Images showing metabolic activity using a radioactive tracer.
Images of the body produced using high-frequency sound waves.
Image made using radiation to view bones and tissues.
Listening to body sounds, often with a stethoscope.
Force of blood against the walls of arteries.
The weight-to-height ratio used for estimating body fat.
The measure of the body's internal heat level.
The swelling caused by excess fluid in tissues.
Visual examination of the body for any abnormalities.
The percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen in blood.
Feeling body structures with hands to assess them.
Tapping the body surface to assess underlying organs.
The number of heartbeats per minute at rest.
The degree of movement possible at a joint.
Involuntary response of the body to a stimulus.
The number of breaths taken per minute at rest.
The basic measurements of the body's essential functions.
Removal of a small tissue sample for examination.
Removal of bone marrow tissue for laboratory testing.
Heart function measured during physical exertion and exercise.
An endoscopic examination of the colon and rectum.
Ultrasound imaging of the heart's structure and function.
A recording of the heart's electrical activity over time.
Visual exam of internal organs using a flexible scope.
Needle insertion into the spinal canal to collect fluid.
A cervical cell sample screened for cellular abnormalities.
Needle removal of fluid from the abdominal cavity.
A test measuring lung airflow and lung volume.
Needle removal of fluid from the pleural space.
The programmed cell death of cells in the body.
Cells that show abnormal size or shape changes.
A growth that is not cancerous or invasive.
The study of individual cells under a microscope.
The abnormal development or maturation of body cells.
The study of tissues and organs under a microscope.
The microscopic examination of diseased tissue in patients.
Increase in the number of cells in a tissue.
The body's response to injury or to infection.
A growth that is cancerous and able to spread.
The spread of cancer to distant body sites.
Death of cells or tissue in a living body.
An abnormal new growth of tissue in the body.
Study of disease causes and effects on the body.

subjects.name: Pharmacology Basics
defs: Movement of a drug from its administration site into the bloodstream.
Fraction of a drug dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.
Transport of a drug to its sites of action through bodily fluids.
Length of time a drug concentration remains sufficient for therapeutic response.
Elimination of drugs from the body, mainly through the kidneys.
Oral drug metabolism before reaching systemic circulation, lowering active concentration.
Time required for serum drug concentration to decrease by one half.
Chemical change of a drug into less active or inactive forms, mainly in the liver.
Time after administration when a drug first produces a therapeutic effect.
Time when a drug reaches its maximum serum concentration.
Strength of attraction between a drug and its receptor site.
Drug that binds a receptor and produces a biological response.
Drug that blocks a receptor, preventing an agonist from activating it.
Maximal effect a drug can produce at a receptor.
Molecule that binds to a receptor or other receiving protein.
Way a drug produces its effects on the body.
Drug producing a limited receptor response, less than a full agonist.
How a drug interacts with receptors and body systems to produce effects.
Cellular site where a drug binds to trigger or block a response.
Ratio of the dose producing a therapeutic effect to the dose causing toxicity.
Medicine that relieves pain without necessarily treating its underlying cause.
Medicine that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria.
Medicine that helps prevent blood clots from forming.
Medicine used to treat depression and related mood disorders.
Medicine that blocks histamine to reduce allergy symptoms.
Medicine used to lower or control high blood pressure.
Medicine that relaxes airway muscles to improve breathing.
Anti-inflammatory medicine mimicking hormones from the adrenal cortex.
Medicine that increases urine output to remove excess fluid.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that reduces pain, fever, and inflammation.
Component providing pharmacological activity in a drug product.
Relating to application or administration of drugs to the skin.
Physical form in which a drug is produced and dispensed.
Administration of a medication through the gastrointestinal tract.
Administration of a drug directly into a skeletal muscle.
Administration of a drug directly into a vein.
Administration of medication by any route outside the gastrointestinal tract.
Application of drugs to the skin or mucous membranes.
Administration of a drug into the adipose tissue under the skin.
Topical administration of a drug through a skin patch.
Harm to a patient resulting from drug exposure.
Noxious, unintended, undesired effect occurring at normal drug doses.
An undesired effect produced by a drug at therapeutic doses.
Immune response due to sensitivity to a substance.
Severe, life-threatening reaction causing bronchospasm and low blood pressure.
Reaction between a medication and another substance or condition.
Preventable event that may cause inappropriate medication use or harm.
Secondary effect produced by a drug at therapeutic doses.
Body adaptation requiring higher doses for the same effect.
Harmful effect from excessive drug levels in the body.
